snippet.title: Millions of Americans Now Borrow Money Just to Eat.
snippet.description:
For most of history, debt helped people buy things they couldn't afford yet. Houses. Cars. Businesses. 

Now it's helping millions afford dinner. That sounds like a small change. It isn't. It's one of the clearest signals that something fundamental has shifted underneath the economy.

You can learn a lot about an economy by looking at what people borrow money for. Houses meant optimism. Cars meant opportunity. Groceries tell a very different story.

snippet.title: It Was Never Just About Oil...
snippet.description:
While the headlines are about tankers and oil, the timing of it all tells a different story.

Because right as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz started escalating, something else was happening - trade negotiations between the United States and China were reaching a critical point.

Whether it was tariffs, technology restrictions, or supply chain decoupling, for years, the economic and political relationship between the world’s two largest economies has slowly been unravelling.

And maybe that’s where the truth in this conflict really is.

snippet.title: Private Credit Is Booming... That's The Problem
snippet.description:
Private credit has become one of the fastest-growing corners of finance. 

But underneath the surface, it has some serious issues.

Around 11.5% of private credit loans now include PIK features, which is an increase of more than 72% percent since the end of 2021. 

Meaning instead of paying interest in cash, the unpaid interest gets added to the loan balance, allowing the borrower to postpone payments while the debt continues to grow.

It creates a system where losses can keep growing, while everything still appears healthy on the surface.

snippet.title: Why Being a Millionaire Doesn't Impress Anyone...
snippet.description:
What a millionaire meant in the past versus what it means now isn't the same. The word stayed. Everything else changed.

In 1848, there were about 50 millionaires in the entire United States. Which is roughly 1 in every 84,000 households at the time.

That means if you gathered every household in a city the size of modern-day Chicago, you’d find about 13 millionaires.

Now, the average American household has a net worth of over $1 million. That’s the average.

And according to UBS, the United States now has roughly 22 million millionaire households.

Which means roughly 1 in every 6 households in America has a million dollar net worth.

snippet.description:
This is rapidly spreading across private credit. Higher rates are squeezing borrowers to the point where the math stops working.

Now around 11.5% of these loans include PIK features. That’s up more than 72% since 2021.

And on paper, everything still looks fine. The loans are “performing.” Income is still reported. But no cash ever actually came in. PIKs blur that line, and most investors won’t notice until it's too late.

Earlier this year, Fitch recorded 11 default events in a single month. Nearly double the 2025 monthly average.

Of those defaults, 60% had one thing in common. They introduced PIKs first.

And on paper, everything still looks fine. The loans are “performing.” Income is still reported. But no cash ever actually came in. PIKs blur that line, and most investors won’t notice until it's too late.

Earlier this year, Fitch recorded 11 default events in a single month. Nearly double the 2025 monthly average.

Of those defaults, 60% had one thing in common. They introduced PIKs first.

snippet.title: If You Don't Understand Bonds, You Don't Understand Money
snippet.description:
Stocks can ignore reality. The bond market tells the real story. 

Bond yields aren't some obscure Wall Street metric. They're the price investors demand to lend money. When that price rises everywhere, something underneath the system is fundamentally changing.

Your mortgage rate, your car loan, the return on your savings: none of it was decided by your bank. It was decided in the bond market. 

It's the thing every other price answers to.

snippet.title: Why Gen Z and Millennials Can't Catch Up
snippet.description:
The challenge facing the younger generations isn't just that homes are more expensive.

It's that many of the assets responsible for creating wealth over the last few decades have become increasingly difficult to buy into.

So while existing owners got richer, younger Americans found themselves increasingly locked out of the very assets that create the wealth.

snippet.title: Everyone Thinks The Interest Rate Story Is Over... It's Just Started
snippet.description:
One of the biggest misconceptions about interest rates is that they impact the economy immediately.

They don't.

When the Federal Reserve raises rates, the effects don't show up overnight. They ripple through the financial system slowly. If you want to understand where higher interest rates are really landing, you have to follow the money.

You have to look at who borrowed when money was cheap, who needs to refinance today, and who suddenly has to survive in a world where capital isn't free anymore.

And right now, there's one asset class that's starting to feel that pain more than anyone else.

snippet.title: The (Hidden) Problem With America's New Millionaires
snippet.description:
The average American's net worth is increasingly tied to paper gains that can disappear as quickly as they appeared.

And for households worth between $1 and $2 million, U.S. Census Bureau data shows that 39% of their net worth sits in their primary residence and 33% sits in their retirement accounts.

Which means a job loss, medical emergency, or market correction can expose just how fragile that wealth really is.

And that's the difference.

snippet.title: Most People Think Bonds are Boring... Economists Think They're a Crystal Ball
snippet.description:
Bond yields measure what investors think comes next. Each maturity sending a different signal about the economy.

It's where the market hides its opinions about the future.

Every maturity is a different gauge measuring growth, inflation, interest rates, and trust.

The two-year predicts Fed policy. The ten-year helps set the price of money. The thirty-year asks whether investors still trust the long-term plan.

snippet.title: Millionaires Don't Look Like Millionaires Anymore
snippet.description:
The average millionaire isn't driving a Lamborghini or vacationing on a yacht.

Instead today, they're probably checking their retirement account and hoping the housing market doesn't fall.

Because roughly 72% of the average millionaires wealth today, is tied up in long-term illiquid assets. Assets they cannot easily access.

And that’s how we created a new type of millionaire. 

The ones that are balance sheet rich, but cash flow poor.
